I have been working this land for 40 years. I know my soil and my weather. Two households, just my wife and me now, so I cannot do the heavy work like I used to. I have to be smart about what I plant and where.

My 10.1 mu splits naturally: 7 mu for my wheat-maize rotation on the main fields, and 3.1 mu for cotton on the sandier ground near the edge where the rotation does not do as well. This is how I have always done it.

**Wheat:** I plant in October after the maize comes off. I use an improved variety — the local agricultural station has been pushing Jimai varieties and I have had good results. I do not trust hybrid wheat. I apply compound fertilizer at planting and top-dress urea at jointing. I pump from the well three times: once before winter sets in, once at jointing, once at grain filling. Powdery mildew and aphids are my main worries so I spray three times. I use rotary tillage now — deep ploughing is too hard on the back at my age.

**Maize:** Right after wheat harvest in June, I direct-seed hybrid maize — no tillage, straight into the stubble. This saves time and the soil is already loose. I top-dress urea twice. I only pump water if summer rains fail — usually twice is enough. One herbicide pass, one spray for corn borer.

**Cotton:** I plough in spring and transplant seedlings. Cotton takes the most work and most pesticides — bollworm, spider mites, aphids, whitefly. I spray five times through the season. I irrigate three times from the well. Cotton income matters for the household, so I keep the 3.1 mu.
